I’m glad you’re checking the migration first! From a safety‑first standpoint, it’s usually best to **err on the side of caution** when a migration touches production data—especially one that drops a table that stores your users. Here’s what you should consider: | What the migration does | Why it matters | What to check before allowing it | |------------------------|----------------|-----------------------------------| | **`DROP TABLE users;`** | Removes the whole table and **all rows**. | • Do you have a recent, tested backup of your database?
• Is the table the only place customers’ data lives? | | **`CREATE TABLE users (...)`** | Creates a brand‑new table, but nothing is moved automatically. | • Are you re‑creating the same structure (columns, types, indexes)?
• Will any automatic data insertion (e.g., the `created_at` default) work? | | **Data migration script (if any)** | If the migration includes statements to repopulate the table, it must succeed. | • Did you review those INSERT/SELECT statements?
• Do they reference existing tables/data that won’t be present because of the `DROP`? | | **Trigger / Permission changes** | Dropping a table removes all triggers, foreign‑key constraints, and role permissions. | • Are any other parts of your app dependent on those? | | **None of the above** | In other words, the drop + recreate is *irreversible* without a backup. | • Do you have a rollback plan (e.g., a copy of the old table or a point‑in‑time restore)? | ### Quick decision checklist 1. **Do you have a full database backup?** *If not, grab one immediately.* 2. **Is this migration for a feature the customers are using?** *If the users table already holds real customer data, dropping it will delete every accounts record.* 3. **Will the migration script include code to copy the data back?** *If not, you’ll lose all records.* 4. **Have you reviewed the migration with a developer or DBA?** *Even if you’re not a developer, a colleague who can read SQL will be invaluable.* If any of those boxes are “No”, it’s safer to **re‑think or postpone** the migration. ### What to do if you decide to proceed (only if you're sure) - **Run the migration in a staging environment first.** Test the drop‑create sequence, data copy, and application functionality before applying it in production. - **Use a transaction.** Wrap the drop and create in a transaction so that if something fails, it rolls back and you don’t end up with an empty `users` table. - **Keep the backup.** If anything goes wrong, you’ll want to restore from the snapshot you took earlier. ### Bottom line If you’re not 100% certain that the migration preserves or restores the user data, **do not run it in production**. The best practice is to get a backup, test in a non‑live environment, and confirm that everything comes back exactly as it was (or better) before letting it touch real customers. --- **If you need more detail**—or you’d like me to walk you through checking the migration script or setting up a backup—just let me know!
